newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia cuts minimum term on Tbill-related forwards.
newsitem.headline: Russia cuts minimum term on Tbill-related forwards.

text.p: Russia's central bank said on Tuesday it was cutting from December 5 the guaranteed yield for non-residents holding government securities to maturity to 13 percent from 16 percent.

The central bank is also cutting the minimum term for forward transactions for non-residents repatriating proceeds from government securities operations to two months from three months and the minimum term for similar option contracts to four months from six months, First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told a news conference.
"These (changes) are the result of the stability of the currency and the success of the Eurobond," he said.

Aleksashenko said the central bank was setting a limit of $1 billion on non-resident purchases of government securities in December, the same as in November. The limits are indicative and can be changed in the light of circumstances during the month.
"We will continue our policy of equalising conditions for non-residents and residents," he said.

Since mid-August non-residents have been able to open special rouble "S" accounts at designated Russian banks, and to use funds in these accounts to buy T-bills and government bonds at auctions, and trade in the secondary market.
Non-residents can repatriate funds from these accounts only through forward and option deals with a minimum term, which has now been cut.
The Russian banks must offset part of these transactions with the central bank, at special rates which allow the central bank to cap the guaranteed dollar yield to foreigners.

The guaranteed yield applies only to shorter securities bought at auction and held to maturity. Non-residents buying longer-term paper or trading aggressively in the secondary market, can lock in higher yields.
The Russian authorities, anxious to avoid a sudden outflow of hot money, have said they will gradually liberalise this scheme.
In recent weeks the central bank has cut the proportion of offsetting deals on spot purchases of roubles and forward sales of roubles to 75 from 90 percent.

The authorities confirmed earlier on Tuesday that the current rouble policy will be continued throughout 1997. This involves depreciating the rouble in line with inflation by setting daily upper and lower limits, known as the "sloping corridor".
